readerTitle: The $900 question: why good sellers ask before they pitch
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 단체 예약, B2B 일정 관리 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격을 정하는 것은 당신의 설명이 아니라 고객의 문제다. 질문으로 문제를 먼저 찾아야 제안할 내용과 받을 가격이 정해진다.
misconception: 고객이 가격을 물으면 바로 답하고, 상품을 잘 설명할수록 잘 판다. 비싸다는 반응이 나오면 할인이 해법이다.

sources.text: 영업 교육의 일반 원리 (진단 후 제안, 상담형 영업)

factChecks.note: 외부 연구 통계(예: 영업 통화 분석, 말하기 비율 데이터)는 정확성 확인이 어려워 의도적으로 넣지 않았습니다. 관련 연구는 SAL-02-09(Xerox 사례)에서 다룹니다.
고객사 예산 $3,500은 가상 설정입니다. 제안 금액 $3,100이 예산 안에 들어가는지 확인했습니다.

cards.title: Same phone call. Two endings. $900 apart.
body: A company calls a restaurant: "How much for a dinner for 40 people?"
One manager answers with a price. The other answers with a question. The second one books a bigger event, at a higher price, without giving a discount.

image.label: Two restaurant managers on the phone, one talking, one listening
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면을 반으로 나눠 왼쪽은 메뉴판을 들고 말풍선을 쏟아내는 매니저, 오른쪽은 메모장에 적으며 듣는 매니저. 오른쪽 위에 작은 "+$900" 태그. 실제 식당 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: "How much for 40 people?"
body: You manage a restaurant with a private room. Your set menus run $55, $65 and $80 per person.
A caller wants a company dinner for 40 next month. Their first question is the price. What do you say first?

options.text: Quote the popular $65 menu and offer to email the details
options.feedback: Fast and clear, and the caller asked for it. But you're guessing what they need, and a bare number invites a "that's a bit much."

options.text: Say prices depend on the evening, then ask what the dinner is for
options.feedback: You delay the number by a minute. In return you learn what this dinner has to achieve, which tells you what to offer and what it's worth.

options.text: Walk them through all three menus so they can choose
options.feedback: It feels helpful and thorough. But you're pitching before you know the problem, so most of what you say won't matter to them.

cards.title: What the questions found.
body: The first manager quoted $65. The caller hesitated, so he dropped to $55: **$2,200**.

The second asked what the evening was for. Answers: the CEO is giving a speech, half the team is vegetarian, and the budget is $3,500. She offered the $70 menu with a vegetarian option, plus the private room.

cards.title: Questions before pitches
body: **Questions before pitches** means you learn the customer's situation and problem before you present anything. A doctor examines you before writing a prescription. A good seller works the same way.
The caller asked about price, but price wasn't the real issue. A speech that nobody can hear was. Until you know the problem, any pitch is a guess, and a guess is easy to haggle over.

image.label: Doctor-style diagnosis: questions first, then the offer
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 흐르는 인포그래픽. "Ask" (물음표 아이콘 세 개) → "Find the problem" (돋보기) → "Offer" (선물 상자). 반대 순서 화살표에는 X 표시와 "Guess" 라벨.

cards.title: Three things questions do that pitches can't.
body: Good questions are about the customer, not your product: what it's for, what goes wrong today, what happens if it goes wrong.
list: **You pitch less, and better:** you mention only what solves their problem
**They hear their own reasons:** "a quiet room for the speech" is their idea, not your upsell
**Objections come out early:** you learn the budget before you name a price
cards.callout: A price feels high when it's compared to nothing. It feels fair when it's compared to the problem.

cards.title: It works wherever someone asks "how much?"
body: A plumber asked for a quote on a new tap can ask how old the pipes are and what's been leaking. The answer may turn a $150 job into the repair the homeowner actually needs.
Inside a company, a manager asking the finance team for budget can first ask what finance worries about this year. The same request, framed around their concern, gets a different hearing.

cards.title: Questions can become an interrogation.
body: Some customers know exactly what they want. A regular ordering the usual, or a buyer comparing two clear quotes, wants a straight answer. Holding back the price can feel like a trick.

Ask a few questions that matter, and say why you're asking: "So I can suggest the right menu." Never ask what you could have looked up. And don't use leading questions to steer people. Customers notice, and trust drops fast.

cards.title: Now it's a software demo.
body: You sell scheduling software to clinics and salons. A salon owner books a 30-minute demo. Your product has 20 features, and your team's usual demo shows all of them.
How do you use the 30 minutes?

options.text: Run the full feature tour, then leave time for questions
options.feedback: It shows everything the product can do. But the owner has to work out which parts matter, and most of the 30 minutes goes to features they'll never use.

options.text: Spend the first 10 minutes on how they book now and what goes wrong
options.feedback: You give up a third of the demo time. In return, if no-shows cost them money, you show reminders and deposits, not 20 features.

options.text: Send a recorded demo and the price list so they can decide alone
options.feedback: It respects their time and some buyers prefer it. But you lose the chance to learn their problem, so they judge you only on price.

cards.title: Find the problem before you name the price.
body: A pitch made before you understand the customer is a guess. A few good questions turn it into an answer, and answers are harder to haggle over.
**Try it today:** write down three questions you could ask a new customer before you describe anything you sell. Use them on the next call.
